newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: First BSE case found in Netherlands.
newsitem.headline: First BSE case found in Netherlands.

text.p: The Netherlands on Friday reported its first case of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease.
"I have the worst news that any agriculture minister can have," Dutch farm minister Jozias van Aartsen told Dutch television.
"The Netherlands was until now an island free of this disease. With great regret I have to announce that this is no longer the case."

A ministry spokesman confirmed that this was the first case of the brain-wasting disease -- linked to a new strain of the fatal Creutzfeld-Jacob disease in humans -- to be identified in The Netherlands.
Piet van Dijk told Reuters that the pregnant cow, which had been born in The Netherlands five years ago and had never been out of the country, was identified as contaminated on March 11.
Subsequent laboratory testing had confirmed the diagnosis on Friday, he added.

He said that the entire herd at the farm in Wilp in the central Netherlands, comprising 60 dairy cows and 50 calves, would be slaughtered on Saturday as a precautionary measure and their remains examined for possible contamination.
A ministry spokeswoman said later the farm would be sealed off and the cow's parentage and offspring traced and vetted.
Other meat at the abattoir where the cow had been slaughtered had already been destroyed, Sandra Slagboom said.
"These are the measures that have been agreed so far," she said. "More steps could follow depending on what we find."
Van Aartsen said he had contacted European Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler and some of his European Union colleagues to keep them informed of developments.
"We will leave no stone unturned to get to the bottom of this," he said.
Slagboom said that experts were working on the assumption that the disease had been transmitted through contaminated fodder or from cow to calf.

In Britain, where the vast majority of cases have been identified until now, BSE has been linked to cattle fodder made with animal remains and thought to carry scrapie, a similar disease found in sheep.
Slagboom said that the Netherlands had banned fodder containing animal remains from being fed to ruminants as a precaution in the late 1980s.
Such fodder had however been assumed not to contain scrapie because it was produced under much higher temperatures and at a much higher pressure than in Britain, she added.

Last year The Netherlands ordered the precautionary slaughter and incineration of 64,000 calves imported from Britain in a decision slammed by many of its European partners at the time as an over-reaction.

The Dutch meat commodities board said that all cattle for slaughter are rigorously checked by independent veterinary experts at the abattoir and it was "absolutely impossible" that any BSE-contaminated meat could enter the food chain.
Since the initial discovery of the disease in 1986, some 178,000 BSE cases have been confirmed in the European Union and Switzerland, according to European Commission figures.
"In the Netherlands we have found only one case -- we are hoping it stays that way," Van Aartsen said.
